_libro.subtitulo: A look at its geological wonders
_libro.lema: “Geositios de Chile: una mirada a sus maravillas geológicas” (Geosites of Chile: A Look at Its Geological Wonders) is a book that seeks to share the extraordinary geological diversity and richness of our country. Geosites are small chapters of the vast and fascinating natural history of Chile and the planet. They are our heritage, and they must also be our legacy.
_libro.pie_portada: view to the northwest of the Cerro Castillo geosite. The rock wall shows the different geological units that make it up, partly covered by snowfields or sediment. At the bottom, a glacial lake. Photo: Felipe Andrade A.

prologos.titulo: Foreword by the National Director of Sernageomin, Patricio Aguilera Poblete
prologos.texto: An important part of our mission as the National Geology and Mining Service is to generate, maintain and disseminate information on basic geology and on the geological resources and hazards of the national territory, serving the country's development and the well-being and safety of the community. That is why this book, which describes and organizes part of our geological heritage, is consistent with our institutional mission. “Geosites of Chile, a look at its geological wonders” was born from the interest, effort and vision of Sernageomin's professionals to share with society the extraordinary geological diversity and richness of our country. Going through these pages and exploring each of the 49 geosites described will give us a new look at geological phenomena that have shaped and configured our territory, representing various processes that occurred during its geological evolution, from the Paleozoic era to the present, including aspects related to the origin and evolution of life on Earth. However, the importance of some of these places is not only due to the geoscientific knowledge we have about them: their links to historical events or ancestral knowledge, their well-known recreational or tourist use, or their role in supporting knowledge of diverse ecosystems throughout our country give them greater relevance and bring them closer to people and communities. We invite everyone to enjoy this book, which offers the chance to know, appreciate and value even more the diversity of our territory, and to raise awareness of how we occupy it and develop within it, especially at this stage of human evolution in which we face significant global changes that are increasingly frequent and severe. Finally, in a task shared with other institutions, above all the prestigious Geological Society of Chile, we hope this book will contribute to the recognition of these and other places relevant to the geosciences, which belong to the diverse and vast natural heritage of our country, and that it will therefore also help generate and activate the conservation measures they deserve.

prologos.titulo: Foreword by the President of the Geological Society of Chile, Millarca Valenzuela Picón
prologos.texto: “Geosites of Chile, a look at its geological wonders” arrives at a critical moment for Chile, in the year when many families lost their homes, built in flood zones that had been dry for many years, along almost every river in south-central Chile, and with the shocking case of the sinkholes in the Concón Dunes, one of the geosites in this book. The climate crisis is already here, hitting us hard with material damage and loss of life that could be avoided if the whole chain of public and private institutions responsible for building understood that territories at high risk of disaster should not be used for that purpose, as technical agencies such as Sernageomin advise. These cases lead us to reflect that we need political leaders, business people and state officials who better understand the aspects of geoscience that affect society, and also citizens who know the territories they inhabit so they can live in them more safely. During my work in Sernageomin's Geoheritage Unit in 2018, I was in charge of the first steps toward this book, conceived as one of the first tasks under the framework agreement signed between Sernageomin and the Geological Society of Chile to collaborate on the geoheritage issues both institutions share. The aim was a book that would help spread the geological richness of the country, with emblematic sites that citizens could identify with (Morro de Arica, Cerro Dragón Dune, La Portada and others), but also more remote ones, to make them known and show how these places can tell small or great stories of planet Earth. The synoptic map of the geosites on the geological time chart included in the book, together with the geological context in which they all appear, offers a pleasant way to discover the stories each one tells, which in turn helps us better understand the geology of the places where we live, which have undergone incredible processes and transformations, leaving traces that we must then decipher. I invite you to enjoy and marvel at these magnificent representatives of the more than 500 geosites currently in the repositories of Sernageomin, the Geological Society of Chile and other institutions, which we hope will keep growing and raising awareness of the territory that nourishes our lives, so that we can enjoy it and also make better decisions about how to live in it.

g01: Top: view west of the village of Ancuta near the Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite, Arica y Parinacota Region. Bottom: the Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite. On the right, brown and ochre layers of lake sediments and whiter layers of volcanic ash. In the background, among clouds, Guallatiri volcano. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g02: View north-northeast of the city of Arica from the Morro de Arica geosite. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: general view south of the Morro de Arica. Source: © Photographic Archive of the National Monuments Council, 2008. Photo: Karina Sánchez V.
Bottom: pillow lava structures in the middle of the western slope of the Morro de Arica, notable for their rough texture and oval shapes. Photo: Guillermo López A., Sernageomin.
g03: Top: view east of the red lagoon of Amuyo, Arica y Parinacota Region. Bottom: view east of the red lagoon, showing the salt crusts of different colors that give the lagoons of this geosite their hues. Photo: Francisco Munita Y.
g04: Top: view northwest of the Cerro Dragón Dune and the city of Iquique. Bottom: view south of the dune, with its sharp, winding crest in the center; on the left, the imposing coastal cliff about 500 m high, and on the right, Iquique on the coastal platform. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g05: View west of the rough crust of the Pintados salt flat, with the interpretation center and the slopes bearing the geoglyphs. Photo: Felipe Fuentes C., Sernageomin.
Top: view west of the Pintados geoglyphs.
Bottom: gypsum layer in the salt crust near the interpretation center.
g06: Top: view west of Los Puquios of the Llamara Salt Flat from a boardwalk viewpoint, with an information panel about the salt flat and the puquios in the foreground. Bottom: microbial mat at the geosite. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g07: View east of the geysers, the episodic hydrothermal eruptions typical of the El Tatio geothermal system. Photo: Daniela Montecinos C.
Top: a thermal feature where a jet of water and gas bursts from inside the Earth.

Bottom: close-up of a siliceous sinter deposit with a filament texture, linked to colonies of thermophilic bacteria that feed on sulfur and become trapped in the forming silica crust. This type of biogenic deposit is also called a microbialite.
g08: Top: view southeast of La Portada and part of the coastal cliff, with the city of Antofagasta in the background. Photo: Renate Wall Z. Bottom: view southeast of the geosite. On the left, the cliff shows dark volcanic rocks at its base and, above them, light-colored fossil-bearing sedimentary layers. Photo: Marcela Ávalos V.
g09: Top: satellite view of the Monturaqui Impact Crater. SkySat image, RGB 3-2-1 (natural color). Source: Monturaqui Crater, Antofagasta Region, Chile, Mar 21, 2023. Planet Labs PBC. All rights reserved. © 2023; Esri, Chile. Bottom: view of the eastern side of the crater. Photo: Flaviu Petru C.
g10: Top: handmade sign calling for the appreciation and conservation of the Orbicular Tonalite, made by students of Colegio Caldera. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: view west of the orbicular tonalite. The spotted look comes from about 196 orbicules per square meter.
Bottom: the orbicules consist of a dioritic core and a dark, partly radial shell. Between them is granodiorite with pale pink potassium feldspar.
g11: View north of Los Dedos Paleontological Park, with fossil-bearing rock layers and the park's trails in the foreground. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: along the trails you can see layers of the Bahía Inglesa Formation with abundant fossils visible to the naked eye.
g12: View northeast of Quebrada Pinte. The red and yellow strata are fossil-bearing sandstones and limestones of the Lautaro Formation. Photo: Felipe Coloma B., Sernageomin.
Top: view east of Lautaro Formation strata, tilted 70° to the west. Photo: Felipe Coloma B., Sernageomin.
g13: Top left: replica of a titanosaur (Antarctosaurus wichmannianus), whose fossil bones were found at this site. Top right: replica of a person of the Molle culture, whose people occupied this cave about 9,000 years ago. Bottom: view north of Casa de Piedra. The cave's rock overhang is an intrusive sill, more resistant to weathering than the sedimentary rocks below it. Photo: Felipe Fuentes C., Sernageomin.
g14: Top: marine abrasion terraces on the coast of Fray Jorge National Park, from the mouth of the Limarí River northward. Terraces are marked with a horizontal line and the letter T with their level number. Bottom: mouth of the Limarí River, showing the estuary and the terraces continuing south. Photo: Felipe Fuentes C., Sernageomin.
g15: View northwest of the Quereo Dunes, with the typical coastal vegetation of the area. Photo: Daniela Villela O., Sernageomin.
Top: the sand accumulation zone (lee side) of a barchan dune.
g16: Top: view northeast of Rano Kao crater, one of the island's most prominent landforms. Bottom: view south of the crater from the viewpoint of the same name. The lake in the crater, in the center of the photo, is environmentally vital for the island and valuable for studying climate change over the last 37,000 years. Source: karkozphoto, Envato Elements, 2021.
g17: Top: view southeast from the village of Hierro Viejo. The Devil's Staircase is at the top of the hill, in the rock cliff center-left. Bottom: view southwest of the dike known as the Devil's Staircase, on a hillside southeast of Hierro Viejo. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g18: Quirilluca coastal cliff. In the center, at the base of the cliff, one of the caves carved by the sea. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: different rock layers of Pliocene age can be seen at the cliff, some containing fossils of mollusks and vertebrates.
g19: Top: view north of one of the dune crests at Concón. In the background, buildings whose construction has reduced the original dune field. Bottom: view north of the dune field, with ripple marks in the foreground, which form perpendicular to the prevailing wind. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g20: Top: intrusive rock with columnar jointing on the western slope of Cerro Santa Lucía, with part of Santiago behind. Bottom: the hill's architecture and walkways take advantage of the rock's columnar structures, giving special beauty to this geographic and cultural landmark of Santiago. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g21: Top: view east of the plates and San José volcano (background) from Lo Valdés. Photo: Rodrigo Mardel H. Bottom: view southeast of the Lo Valdés Plates. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g22: Top: Quebrada Las Amarillas seen from route G-25 toward El Morado Natural Monument. Photo: Víctor Godoy D. Bottom: view southwest of the ravine. At lower right, the lower part of its alluvial fan, crossed by route G-25. Photo: Mónica Marín D., Sernageomin.
g23: View southeast from Machalí showing the Pudahuel Ignimbrite beside the Carretera del Cobre (route H-25). Photo: Alejandro Alfaro S., Sernageomin.
Top: section of the Pudahuel ignimbrite up to 5 m thick, exposed in a road cut on route H-25 near Machalí.
g24: Top: the fossil footprints attract many tourists every year. Bottom: view east of the dinosaur tracks and the bed of the Baños del Flaco Formation. Photo: Paulina Arellano C.
g25: Top: view southeast of the El Fierro Fault. Bottom: diagram of the rock units and the El Fierro Fault (blue line) with its relative movement (yellow arrows). Dashed yellow lines mark contacts between units and light-blue lines show the attitude of some layers. Photo: Paulina Arellano C. Geological interpretation modified from Mescua et al. 2013.
g26: Top: view southwest of the beach and rocks of Constitución, with the Piedra de la Iglesia in the center. Photo: Jessica Leiva M. Bottom: view southwest of the Piedra de la Iglesia, the natural symbol of Constitución. Photo: Andrés Muñoz V.
g27: Aerial view of La Leona waterfall in Radal Siete Tazas National Park after the February 2010 earthquake. Photo: Manuel Arenas A., Sernageomin.

Left: two of the seven 'cups', with pools and small waterfalls. Photo: Andrés Muñoz V. Right: the same place after the February 2010 earthquake, when water stopped flowing through the pools. Photo: Mónica Marín D., Sernageomin.
g28: Top: view northeast of the rock wall at La Cárcel, with the vertical rock columns that give the geosite its name at the bottom. Bottom: view from above of the imposing columns, very popular for rock climbing. Photo: Yvanel Aravena B.
g29: General view of Los Pincheira Cave, showing the entrance and part of the overhang of volcanic rocks forming the wall. Photo: José Naranjo S.
Top left: close-up of the entrance wall, showing the irregular fracturing of the lavas. Photo: José Naranjo S.
Top right: side view of the entrance, with irregular fracturing of the lavas and part of the 20 m waterfall. Photo: José Naranjo S.
g30: View east of the Cobquecura Stone Church with some visitors. Photo: Francisca Salazar D.
Left: view east from the vault of the Stone Church. Right: close-up of its rocks, with an iron-oxide patina from the oxidation of mafic minerals. Photo: Francisca Salazar D.
g31: View from above of Los Pangues Grotto. In the right foreground, the volcanic rock layer that forms the roof. Photo: Rayén Rivera V.
Left: view west of the grotto, showing the different volcanic layers and the more resistant roof. Photo: Rayén Rivera V.
g32: Top left: marine invertebrate fossils in sandstones of the Quiriquina Formation (Late Cretaceous). Photo: Ricardo Velásquez H., Sernageomin. Top right: plesiosaur fossils, the most representative marine reptile of the end of the Cretaceous. Photo: Roberto Merino G. Bottom: sedimentary rocks at Caleta Cocholgüe; below, yellowish-gray sandstones of the Quiriquina Formation and above them sandstones of the Curanilahue Formation (Early Eocene). A normal fault (center) dropped the right block relative to the left. Photo: Roy Fernández J.
g33: Top: view north of the folds, with Antuco volcano on the left. Geological interpretation: Juan Pablo Contreras F., Sernageomin. Bottom: the Curamallín Overturned Anticline from the Los Pinos River ravine looking north, with the parts of the overturned folds labeled. Photo: Paulo Urrutia B. Geological interpretation: Juan Pablo Contreras F.
g34: View east from Piedra del Águila over the araucaria forest of Nahuelbuta National Park. Photo: Francesc Ferraro C.
Top: panoramic view of Piedra del Águila. Wooden stairs lead up to the park's main viewpoint.
g35: Top left: advancing front of the lava from the Navidad cone; the person at the bottom gives a sense of the flow front's height and block size. Top right: view north-northeast of the Lolco River valley, with the lava from the Navidad cone advancing in December 1988 on the left. Photo: Renate Wall Z. Bottom: view north of the Navidad cone in the Nalcas National Reserve, with the snowy summit of Lonquimay stratovolcano behind. Photo: Patricio Contreras F.
g36: Top: view west of volcanic strata from Llaima eruptions at Truful-Truful Canyon. Each layer represents a volcanic process linked to an eruption, from oldest at the base to youngest at the top. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin. Bottom: view southwest of the canyon. Source: Galyna_Andrushko, Envato Elements, 2021.
g37: Aerial view north of Villarrica volcano, or Ruka Pillañ, with its characteristic cover of glaciers and snow; Lanín volcano behind. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: the summit crater of Villarrica at 2,820 m a.s.l., one of seven volcanoes in the world with a lava lake inside. Photo: Cristian Ramírez S.
Bottom right: explosion in the lava lake of Villarrica's crater. The lake is highly dynamic, changing depth and producing frequent explosions. Photo: Claudia Bucarey
g38: Top left: hardened sand (cancagua) was used as foundations and bricks in the walls and fortifications of Fuerte Niebla. Top right: excavation of the cancagua by the Spanish reveals sand layers from coastal dunes active more than 40,000 years ago. Photo: Carolina Miralles G.

Cancagua layers in the coastal cliff representing three Middle to Late Pleistocene coastal environments: A: beach and intertidal sands; B: estuarine silts and sands; C: coastal dune sands. Photo and geological interpretation: Rodrigo Vega S.
g39: View northwest toward Villarrica volcano, with lavas of the 1971 eruption in the Chaillupén stream in the foreground. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: a lava block about 2 m high with the sharp edges typical of aa lava.
g40: View northeast from route T-709 showing the lake and one flank of the Carrán maar crater, with the bare summit of the Mirador cone behind. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin
Top: view east of the Mirador cone from route T-709 between Lago Ranco and Rupameica Alto. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
g41: Excavation area of the Pilauco site, looking south along Río Cachapoal street. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: the museum hall at Parque Pleistoceno Chuyaca, highlighting the extinct megafauna found at Pilauco.
g42: View north of the Petrohué River, its falls and the footbridge that lets you see this geosite up close. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: the Petrohué River cascading over lavas from Osorno volcano.
g43: Top: aerial view of Chaitén town hit by the secondary lahar after the 2008 eruption of Chaitén volcano. Photo: Álvaro Amigo R., Sernageomin. Bottom: the Chaitén caldera today, with lava domes and continuous steam emission from several points. Photo: Paul Duhart O., Sernageomin.
g44: Top: from the colorful stillness of Aysén's Patagonia rise the steep towers which, with the glaciers, give Cerro Castillo its character. Source: Sernatur Aysén. Bottom: view northwest of Cerro Castillo partly covered by snowfields. Below, a turquoise lagoon fed by glacial meltwater. Photo: Felipe Andrade A.
g45: Top: dissolution of the marble has created countless striking shapes and islets. Bottom: the colorful rocks of the Marble Chapel shine through and reflect in the turquoise waters of Lake General Carrera. Photo: Paula Alarcón C., Sernageomin.
g46: Left: view north of Piedra Clavada, evidence of the explosive volcanism in what is now the Aysén Region during the Jurassic-Cretaceous. Photo: José Benado W. Right: Piedra Clavada is a recognized and protected natural landmark of the Aysén Region. Source: Sernatur Aysén.
Top: close-up of Piedra Clavada showing some of its volcanic rock layers.
g47: General view of the Paine massif; on the left, the highest peak, Paine Grande, and next to it the Torres del Paine. Photo: Andrés Muñoz V.
Top: the Torres del Paine from the Base Torres viewpoint. Photo: Marcos Aguilar N.
Bottom right: close-up of the three granite columns forming the Torres del Paine. Photo: Lorenzo Albertini.
g48: Sign pointing the way to the Pali-Aike Cone, visible as gentle hills on the horizon. Photo: Marcos Aguilar N.

Top left: aerial view southwest of the Pali-Aike Cone. Its steep walls soften to the north, giving its characteristic horseshoe shape. Source: Filmagallanes, a project run by Corfo and funded by the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica Regional Government.

Bottom: aerial view of the small volcanic edifice with a circular crater 160 to 180 m across. Source: Filmagallanes, a project run by Corfo and funded by the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica Regional Government.
g49: Top: the Dientes de Navarino and surroundings looking northeast. Photo: Esteban Salazar P., Sernageomin.

Top: view east of the Dientes de Navarino, showing its current glacially shaped landforms. Bottom: the same photo labeled with rock units and geological and geomorphological features. Photo and geological interpretation: Esteban Salazar P., Sernageomin.
